1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.background: Black's most common move after 2.Nf3. It is the gateway to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical Variations, which arise after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the c5-pawn at once and opens the game. After ...cxd4 White recaptures with a knight, trading a central pawn for a flank pawn in return for quick development and open lines for both bishops. Black gets a central pawn majority and the c-file.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+.name: Sicilian Defence: Moscow Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+.background: Also called the Canal–Sokolsky Attack, after Esteban Canal and Alexey Sokolsky, who began playing it in the 1940s. Sokolsky played it twice at the 1947 Chigorin Memorial. Kasparov played it in his game Kasparov versus the World.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+.strategy: Develops with check and prepares castling, a way to sidestep the heavy theory of the open game. White can aim for a clamp on d5 with pawns on c4 and e4 after exchanging the bishop, or for a broad pawn centre built calmly. A sound, low-risk choice.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Delayed Alapin Variation, with d6
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre and takes the c3 square from the b1-knight, which can then no longer help guard e4. That makes e4 a target for Black's development, so White has to look after it before the centre is built. Solid, but slower than the open game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bd3.name: Sicilian Defence: Kopec System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bd3.strategy: Guards e4 and prepares castling, but the bishop stands directly in front of the d-pawn, which cannot advance until the bishop moves. White gives up the sharp open game for a slower build-up, and Black can develop freely.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto: the bishop on g2 will back up e4 and watch the long diagonal. White avoids the sharp open game for slower manoeuvring play, which gives Black time to develop and take space in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit, Deferred Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.b4.strategy: Offers a pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away from d4, so that White can occupy the centre. White gets space and quick development, but is a pawn down, and once Black has taken, the pawn on b4 is an annoyance that eyes c3, where the b1-knight wants to go.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7.name: Sicilian Defence: Moscow Variation, Main Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7.strategy: The main way out of the check: the bishop invites an exchange of light-squared bishops and leaves the b8-knight free for c6. Black gets a solid, compact position and accepts that White keeps the choice of how to use the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6.strategy: Blocks with the natural developing move, but the knight is pinned and cannot yet influence the centre, so Black plans to unpin with the c8-bishop. White can try to trade bishop for knight and double Black's pawns, or keep the tension and castle.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nd7.strategy: Blocks the check with the knight, which is then pinned to the king and shuts in the c8-bishop. Black avoids the bishop exchange and any doubling of pawns, but the position is cramped, and White can open the centre while Black's development lags.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+.strategy: Exchanges at once: White's bishop, which would be stuck behind a pawn on c4 in the clamp set-up, goes for Black's light-squared bishop. The game becomes quiet and strategic, with both sides fighting over the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.c4.strategy: Puts a pawn on c4 that guards the bishop and, together with e4, controls d5. White commits to a slow, space-gaining game with a clamp on the centre; Black has to find counterplay on the queenside or with piece play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.a4.strategy: Guards the bishop on b5 with a flank pawn so that White need not trade at once. The price is a queenside pawn move that does nothing for the centre, so Black gets time to develop and the game stays slow.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Qxd7.strategy: The sharper recapture. The queen goes to d7 so that the b8-knight keeps its natural square on c6, where it watches d4 and e5 and contests the centre; a knight recapture would give that square up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Nxd7.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which gives up its natural c6 square but keeps the queen at home. Black gets a compact, flexible position with a fianchetto or ...e6 still available, at the price of a slightly passive piece on d7.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Kxd7.strategy: Recaptures with the king, which forfeits castling and leaves the king in the centre for no reason. White can use the time to open lines against it, and Black has two perfectly good recaptures.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Qxd7.strategy: Makes the king safe before anything else and keeps the choice of how to build the centre. The plan is a broad pawn centre against Black's solid set-up, played patiently, since the bishop trade has simplified the position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Qxd7.name: Sicilian Defence: Moscow Variation, Sokolsky Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Bd7 4.Bxd7+ Qxd7.strategy: Takes space and clamps down on d5 with pawns on c4 and e4, so Black has little chance of a freeing ...d5. The cost is a commitment: the pawns are fixed and the game becomes slow and manoeuvring, so Black has to find counterplay by other means.

Develops a piece and guards e4 in advance, but blocks the c-pawn, so the broad pawn centre that White is after cannot be built in the usual way. A sound, ordinary developing move that asks little of Black.
Brings out the knight to its natural square, where it watches d4 and e5. Black meets the coming centre with piece pressure rather than passive defence, and keeps a solid, flexible position.

Attacks the undefended e4 at once, so White has to spend a move on it. A natural developing move with a gain of time; the queen's knight can still come to c6, and Black keeps a solid, flexible position.

Prepares a fianchetto so that the bishop on g7 watches the long diagonal and the centre from a distance. The set-up is compact and sound, but it is slower than developing the knights, and White can build the centre without hindrance.

Prepares the broad pawn centre that White has been aiming for since the bishop trade. The price is that it takes c3 from the b1-knight and e4 still has no defender, so White needs one as soon as Black's knight comes out.

Defends e4 in advance, so a later ...Nf6 gains no tempo, and puts the rook on the file where the centre will open. It keeps the c-pawn free for a broad pawn centre, at the cost of a rook that stands passively until the centre moves.
Develops a piece and guards e4 solidly, but blocks the c-pawn and gives up the broad pawn centre. White settles for a plain developing game that is sound but offers Black little to worry about.

Develops with tempo: the knight attacks the undefended e4, so White must spend a move protecting it before the pawn centre can be completed. Black stands solidly with an equal game and contests the centre by piece play.
Opens the f8-bishop and supports a later ...d5, so Black can contest the centre with a pawn break. The structure is compact and sound; the price is less space, and e4 is not yet troubled.
Builds a fianchetto, with the bishop on g7 pressing on the centre from a distance. Sound but slow: it leaves e4 alone, so White can complete the pawn centre at once and keeps the freer game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles and keeps the bishop on b5, where it still pins the knight, instead of exchanging at once. White makes the king safe, keeps the threat of doubling Black's pawns, and decides the bishop's fate once Black has shown its set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.Bxc6+.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight and doubles Black's pawns on the c-file. In return Black gets the two bishops and a half-open b-file, so White trades a structural plus against the bishop pair: a trade-off that suits patient players.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once while the knight on c6 is pinned, hoping to profit from the pin. Black has no difficulty equalising, and White has traded the patient plan for an open, level game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O Bd7.strategy: Breaks the pin and takes the sting out of an exchange on c6: Black can now recapture with the bishop and keep a healthy pawn structure. White's bishop has lost its target, and White must decide what it is for.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once, but the knight on c6 stays pinned, so White can still exchange on c6 and double Black's pawns. Black gains a tempo, yet the pin is a lasting nuisance, and defending e4 costs White little.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto but leaves the knight pinned, so White can exchange on c6 and double Black's pawns. Black loses time compared with first breaking the pin, and the position is playable but slightly worse.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O Bd7 5..strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre while the bishop stays on b5. White follows a plain strategic plan and Black can develop without risk, since the exchange on c6 no longer doubles anything.

Backs up the bishop on b5 and the e-pawn and prepares an advance in the centre, but commits the queen early and leaves White with a less natural set-up than the plain developing moves. Black has time to complete a sound development.

Guards e4 in advance and clears f1, so the bishop can keep its pin on c6 as long as it is useful and retreat safely when Black questions it. White stays flexible and can build a broad pawn centre without losing the e-pawn.
Develops with tempo: the knight attacks the undefended e4, so White has to spend a move on it before the pawn centre can be built. Black keeps a solid, flexible position.

Asks the bishop at once what it wants. If it takes on c6, Black recaptures with the bishop, which then eyes e4; if it retreats, the pin is gone and Black has gained a useful queenside move. Solid and flexible.

Prepares a compact fianchetto with the bishop on g7. It does not trouble e4, so White has time to build the full pawn centre, and the knight stays pinned while White does so; sound, but White stands a little more freely.
Defends e4 with a developing move, so White can go on building the centre without losing the pawn. It also empties f1, which gives the bishop on b5 a safe retreat once Black questions it.
Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, a solid and safe answer. It gives up the immediate central break, so the game is slow and White's chances are modest.
The queen takes over the defence of e4 and of the bishop on b5, but it is tied to both jobs and leaves the rook without a good file. Black can develop and question the bishop without hindrance.

Puts the question to the bishop. If it takes on c6, Black recaptures with the bishop and has nothing doubled; if it retreats, it has lost its pin and Black has gained a useful queenside move. A solid, flexible set-up for a manoeuvring game.
Opens the f8-bishop and supports a later ...d5, so Black can contest the centre with a pawn break. The position stays compact and solid; the price is some space.
Builds a fianchetto, with the bishop on g7 holding the long diagonal. A compact, sound set-up, but it leaves the bishop on b5 unchallenged and gives White time for the central advance.

Prepares a fianchetto and a compact kingside, with the bishop on g7 to control the long diagonal. For the moment the move also loosens the diagonal towards h8, which is what White's central advance tries to use.

Develops the kingside knight and attacks e4, which ties the queen to its defence. An early e5 only loses a pawn for White, so the knight is well placed to meet the advance that the queen move is aiming at.

Asks the bishop what it wants. If it takes on c6, Black recaptures with the bishop, which then bears on e4 and the queen that must hold it; if it retreats, the pin is gone and Black has gained a useful move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O Bd7 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Moscow Variation, Dorfman Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bb5+ Nc6 4.O-O Bd7 5..strategy: A pawn sacrifice that tries to use the loosened diagonal to h8: after the exchanges on e5 a white queen there would attack the rook. Black can simply take the pawn, and White then has to show the compensation.

Prepares a central pawn break and gives the pawn centre a solid base, while the queen keeps the bishop on b5 guarded. A patient plan that answers the fianchetto in the centre and keeps the space White has.
Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, a safe and modest set-up. It gives up the immediate central break, so Black fianchettoes and develops with a comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with tempo against e4, which the pawn on c3 has left without help from the b1-knight. White must find another defender before the centre can be built, and Black gets an active, comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight to control d4 and e5, ready to challenge the centre White means to build. It does not attack e4, so White can strike with the d-pawn at once, and Black must deal with the pawn tension that follows.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that stops Bb5+ and prepares queenside expansion. It spends a move before developing a piece, so White can set up the pawn centre at once; sound, but a little slow.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2.strategy: Develops and prepares castling while guarding e4 tactically: ...Nxe4 runs into Qa4+, which wins the knight. It keeps the pawn without blocking the plan of a central pawn advance.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Qc2.strategy: Guards e4 with the queen and keeps both bishops flexible, preparing the central advance. It puts the queen out early, and it is a sound plan but less natural than the plain developing moves.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop. A solid, modest set-up that gives up the immediate central break, so the game is slow and Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6.strategy: Develops and adds control of d4 and e5, preparing to meet the central advance with piece pressure. Taking on e4 straight away still fails to Qa4+, so Black first completes development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and keeps a compact pawn chain, ready to meet the central advance with a pawn break of its own. A solid choice that gives up some space for sound development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto, with the bishop on g7 pressing on the centre from a distance. Compact and sound, but slower in challenging the centre, so White gets time to build it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.d4.strategy: The central break that c3 prepared: White challenges the c5-pawn so that a recapture with the c-pawn builds a broad centre on d4 and e4. Black must decide whether to release the tension.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.d3.strategy: The quiet defence of e4: the pawn holds the centre and frees the c1-bishop, but White has given up striking at the centre, and Black can set up in the middle at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.Qc.strategy: Defends e4 from the side and keeps d4 available for the next move. The queen does nothing for development, though, and Black can take the initiative in the centre with ...d5, which hits e4 a second time.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.d4.strategy: Trades the flank pawn for a central one before the centre is supported twice, and opens the c-file for Black. White's recapture leaves pawns on d4 and e4 that Black's pieces can now attack.
Develops with pressure on the knight that guards d4 and e5, but leaves the tension in the centre unresolved. White can capture on c5 or push d5 with gain of time against the knight on c6.

Meets the d4 pawn with a pawn of its own and takes central space. If White captures on e5 the queens face each other on the open d-file and the game simplifies, so Black gets a solid but unambitious position.
Recaptures with the c-pawn and completes the pawn centre that White has aimed at since c3. The open c-file belongs to both sides, and the pawn on e4 still needs watching.
Recaptures with the knight and so drops the plan of a pawn centre. It also leaves e4 unprotected: Black takes it with ...Nxe4, and White must prove compensation for the pawn.
Hangs the queen: Black plays ...Nxd4 and wins it for a knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: Delayed Alapin Variation, Basman-Palatnik Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Be2 Nc6 5.d4.strategy: Grabs the e4 pawn with the king still in the centre. White's d5 at once hits the knight on c6, with Qa4+ in the air along the open diagonal, so Black has to be exact, and the knight on e4 is far from its friends. A risky gambit.

The freeing break. The pawn attacks e4, which is now hit twice, so White must act at once. After exd5 Black recaptures and leaves White with an isolated d4 pawn; after e5 the knight lands on a well-supported e4. Either way the big centre is challenged.
Solid and covers d5, but it passes up the chance to challenge the centre at once. White keeps pawns on d4 and e4, and d5 comes with gain of time against the knight on c6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.g3 b5.name: Sicilian Defence: Kotov Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.g3 b5.strategy: Hangs a pawn for nothing: 4.Bxb5+ wins it with check, since nothing guards b5, and Black has no lead in development to make up for it. White needs only to finish developing, and the quiet g3 set-up is not slow enough to justify a sacrifice.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn and develops a piece in one move. White's bishop is not yet on g2, and once there the knight on f3 blocks it from e4, so White must spend a move defending the pawn while Black develops with no concessions.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5, so that White's d-pawn advance is not free, and keeps the choice between a fianchetto and a central pawn push open. A natural choice: Black waits to see how White commits the kingside pieces before attacking e4.
